t: a district town. A city.

a region. An area containing several towns. (When there are towns in which none has enough people to establish a Sanhedrin in it, as below in halachah 4, one court is established for the whole region - Mirkevet HaMishneh, Lechem Yehudah; and see below 5:1, Rulings and Views.)
those who bear staff and strap. To strike transgressors on the judges' behalf when necessary, and to flog with a strap those liable to lashes (below 16:8).

who go about the markets and the shops, etc.. The officers go around the places of commerce and supervise the prices so that they are not inflated, and check the accuracy of the measures and weights (see Hilchot Gezelah 8:20).

and anything in which they see an indecency, etc.. The officers must also supervise the public so that they do not behave in a way that leads to licentiousness and immodesty (see Hilchot Shevitat Yom Tov 6:21).

But outside the Land of Israel they are not obligated to establish a court in every region. All the more so they are not obligated to establish one in every city (Lechem Yehudah, based on Ramban on Deuteronomy 16:18; and see Meiri, Makkot 7a).
they first establish the Great Court in the Temple. In the Chamber of Hewn Stone (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 5:17).
they sit before the two according to their rank. The other judges sit beside the Nasi and the Av Beit Din according to their order of importance.

whoever is greater than his fellow in wisdom sits closer to the Nasi, on his left, than his fellow. Those greater in wisdom sit on the left of the Nasi, and those lesser than they sit on the right of the Av Beit Din (Radbaz; and the Yad Peshutah explained that the judges are arranged in pairs by rank, the greater of each pair to the left of the Nasi and his fellow to the right of the Av Beit Din).

one at the entrance of the Temple court and one at the entrance of the Temple Mount. These courts served the courts in all the cities of Israel, answering questions about which they were in doubt (see Hilchot Mamrim 1:4).
and it sits in the city gate. In the open area at the entrance to the city where the people would gather and where judges were customarily seated.
they appoint three judges in it. They judge cases of lashes and monetary cases, but have no authority to judge capital cases (below, chapter 5).
so that there will be a majority and a minority, etc.. They appoint an odd number of judges so that it is possible to decide by the majority in case of disagreement.

and one who knows how to listen and knows how to ask and answer. He is not as great as the first, but he understands anything explained to him in the whole Torah, and can discuss it with the first and give his opinion. The other judges must be learned in some of the laws (Kesef Mishneh).
this is a Sanhedrin. A valid Sanhedrin, since it has the minimum number of learned judges required in a Sanhedrin.
the first row is close to the Sanhedrin. The most learned students sit in it.
and in each row they sit according to their rank in wisdom. The wisest sit at the head of the row, and those after them in wisdom sit after them in order of their wisdom.

If the Sanhedrin were divided and needed to ordain one to add to their number. When the case cannot be decided by twenty-three judges and judges must be added, for example when there was a majority of one to convict in a capital case (see below 8:1), or when one of the judges does not know how to decide (below 9:2). The same applies when one of them died and a judge must be ordained in his place to complete the number (Meiri, Sanhedrin 37a; and see Yad Peshutah).

one writes the words of those who acquit and one writes the words of those who convict. If it is necessary to know the reasoning of each one and they do not remember it, the judges' scribes remind them (below 12:3).

so that there will be among them, etc.. A city required to have a Sanhedrin is one with enough people for all the roles needed to run a court system and to fill the essential roles of the city (see Hilchot De'ot 4:23).
and three rows of sixty-nine. The rows of students who sit before the Sanhedrin (above, halachah 7).
and ten idlers of the synagogue. Ten men who do not engage in a trade but remain in the synagogue for the needs of the community (see Hilchot Megillah 1:8).
and two scribes. The judges' scribes.
and two attendants. Court officers who flog those liable to lashes and summon the litigants to judgment (Rashi, Sanhedrin 17b, and see below 16:8; they are the officers mentioned above, halachah 1).
and two zomemin. Two additional men who can testify and refute witnesses in case they are lying.

and two zomemei zomemin. Additional men who can refute the refuting witnesses who are themselves false witnesses. To conduct a trial there must be people able to refute false witnesses, for if there were no possibility of refuting the witnesses, they would not fear to lie (Rashi, ibid.).

and two charity collectors, and one more so that there will be three to distribute the charity. To collect charity (by compulsion) at least two collectors are needed, and to decide how to distribute the charity one more must be added to them, so that there are at least three men, who are considered a court for monetary cases (Hilchot Matnot Aniyim 9:5).
and an expert physician. A skilled physician.
and a scribe. One who engages in the craft of writing.
and a teacher of children. Who teaches them Torah (see also Hilchot Talmud Torah 2:1).
outstanding in Torah wisdom. Distinguished and known for their wisdom.
and calculation of the seasons and constellations and astronomy. Calculating the seasons of the year and the movements of the luminaries and the stars (see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 1:6).
the astrologers. Those who determine which season is good for various actions by looking at the stars (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 11:8).
and the diviners. Fortune-tellers (ibid., halachot 6-7).
and the vanities of idolatry... so that they will know how to judge them. So that they will know whether there is a prohibition and a death penalty for each of the idolatrous practices (ibid. 3:2).
those of established lineage. About whose lineage witnesses have testified (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 20:2).
fit to marry into the priesthood. Whose lineage has no flaw that disqualifies their daughters from marrying priests (such as mamzerim and chalalim).

neither a man very advanced in years nor a eunuch, because they are cruel. Since they have forgotten the pain of raising children or do not expect children, they are hard-hearted and extremely strict in judgment.
nor one who has no children, so that he will be merciful. Who has not yet had children, and has not developed the trait of compassion and mercy.
even though they are not seated in the Sanhedrin. They do not serve as judges in the Sanhedrin.
they judge the people. In monetary cases, in a court of three (Tosafot, Sanhedrin 19a), or even alone (Lechem Mishneh).
and they are judged if there is a claim against them. If there is a suit against them.
lest some mishap come from them. That they will not accept the verdict (see also Hilchot Melachim 3:7).
clean in righteousness. Free of any guilt and of any suspicion.
of gray hair. Elderly.
of tall stature. Tall.
of good appearance. Handsome.
skilled in whispering. Who know how to phrase their words briefly and completely (see Guide of the Perplexed 1:34).
so that the Sanhedrin will not hear through an interpreter. The judges of the court must themselves understand the arguments of the litigants and the witnesses (below 21:8).
each of them must have seven qualities. Ideally, one should seek that they have these traits (Radbaz, Lechem Mishneh).
and the love of people for them. That they be beloved by people.
a good eye. Who is content with what he has (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Avot 5:19).
and a humble spirit. Who does not pursue desires and is not proud or arrogant.
and his youth should have been pleasant. That when he came to his prime, his youth, no bad name came out about him (based on Babylonian Talmud, Ta'anit 16b).
as it says, And Moses stood up and helped them. Moses saved the daughters of Jethro from the shepherds of Midian who oppressed them.
they pursue justice on their own account, by their own understanding. And not only by virtue of their role as judges.
and tranquil. Calm and at ease.
at the entrance of the Temple Mount... at the entrance of the Temple court. To be a judge in the courts located there (see above 1:3).
a convert is disqualified. See also Hilchot Melachim 1:4.
until his mother is from Israel. Then he is fit to judge even if his father is a convert.

which is not so in the Sanhedrin. One blind in one eye is disqualified from the Sanhedrin because he has a blemish (above, halachah 6), a mamzer is disqualified because he cannot marry into the priesthood (above, halachah 1), and a convert whose mother is Jewish and whose father is a convert is also disqualified for capital cases (Kesef Mishneh, and compare Hilchot Yibbum VeChalitzah 4:5; and see also below 11:11).

one blind in both eyes is disqualified for everything. Likewise all those disqualified from testifying, such as women, slaves and minors, are disqualified from judging (Hilchot Edut 16:4; for the details of those disqualified from testifying see ibid. 9:1).
although a court is not less than three. With fewer than three there is no standing of a court.
and two who judged, their judgment is not a judgment. By rabbinic enactment (Kesef Mishneh, Lechem Mishneh and others).
an expert recognized by the public. One whose greatness in Torah and eminence in wisdom is well known to the public (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 1:1, 3:1).
or takes authorization from a court. He received authorization to judge from the Exilarch or from a court in the Land of Israel (ibid. 3:1).
but he is not considered a court. Although his rulings are binding, he does not have the standing of a court for various matters (see below 5:18).
Do not judge alone. Good advice in the way of ethics (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Avot 4:8).
for none may judge alone except One. The Holy One, blessed be He.

a person may take the law into his own hands if he has the power. When a person knows that another owes him money by law, he is not obligated to take him to court, but may take the money due to him without a judgment.

even though there would have been no loss to his property had he delayed and come to court. Taking the law into one's own hands is permitted even where litigating in court would involve no monetary loss.

therefore if his opponent complained against him, etc.. Since it is permitted to take the law into one's own hands, if his opponent complained about him in court, they do not overturn what he did, but judge it as it stands, and only if it becomes clear that the judgment was carried out improperly do they return the money.
as long as they are many. As they add and judge with more judges.

and a wise man is forbidden to sit in judgment until he knows with whom he will sit. This is how a wise man ought to act, and this is how the discerning men of Jerusalem acted (below 22:10). But if it is known that the other judge is a robber or wicked, it is forbidden to join him in judging (ibid.).
and he is found among a conspiracy of traitors. An association of unworthy people.
until when do the judges sit in judgment. During which hours do they sit.
until the end of six hours of the day. Midday.
the Great Court. The Sanhedrin of seventy-one that sat in the Chamber of Hewn Stone.
from the morning tamid. From the time of the slaughter of the daily tamid offering, which is after the whole eastern sky has lit up and before sunrise (Hilchot Temidin UMusafin 1:2).
until the afternoon tamid. Which was offered at nine and a half hours of the day (ibid., halachah 3).
and on Shabbatot and festivals. On which they do not judge (Hilchot Shabbat 23:14).
they would sit in the study hall on the Temple Mount. And not in the Chamber of Hewn Stone, where they sat and judged.
when they need to assemble. And to judge a matter that must be judged by seventy-one judges (see below 5:1 for which matters must be judged by seventy-one).
for the whole time of their sitting. As explained above, halachah 1.
like leprous marks. The priest's examination of leprous marks to declare them impure or pure is done only by day (Hilchot Tumat Tzara'at 9:6).
they do not accept testimony. Since the judges' acceptance of testimony is considered the beginning of a judgment (Kesef Mishneh).
nor do they validate documents. Validating a document is confirming the signatures of the document's witnesses; it is considered a judgment and is done by three judges and by day (Hilchot Edut 6:1).
and in monetary cases, if they began by day it is permitted to finish the judgment at night. But in capital cases they begin and finish by day (below 11:1).
inheritances are like judgments. Bequeathing property by way of inheritance is not like an ordinary transfer of property, but has the standing of a judgment (see Hilchot Nachalot 6:1).

they do not transfer inheritances at night. A person may order his property divided among his heirs unequally if he does so while ill and near death (ibid., halachot 2-4). This act is defined as a judgment, and may be done only by day and not at night.
and he instructed in their presence. How to divide his property among his heirs.

they write but do not make a judgment. Since there are only two, they are not fit to serve as judges and to uphold the dead man's words. But they can be witnesses to his words and write a document serving as testimony of his instruction.
and if there were three... if they wish they make a judgment. Since three can serve as a court, they have the power to act as judges regarding the division of property as the dead man instructed.
with awe and fear, etc.. Out of respect for the Divine Presence (similar to prayer, see Hilchot Tefillah 5:4).
and wrapping. In a tallit (see below, halachah 9).
and it is forbidden to behave lightheadedly, etc.. Similar to a synagogue (ibid. 11:6).
the Sanhedrin or a king or an Exilarch. Those in charge of appointing the judges (see below 4:13-15).
an unworthy judge. One not fit because of his deeds.
for he speaks against the one who is appointed to seat judges. That he should not appoint whomever seems right in his own eyes, but only the worthy.
he is found acquitting the guilty and convicting the innocent. The chosen judge who is not wise and fit.
a pillar. A structure to which people gather for worship (Hilchot Avodah Zarah 7:6).
and in a place of Torah scholars. If he appointed an unworthy judge in a place where there are Torah scholars.
beside the altar of the Lord your God. Beside Torah scholars, who are considered like an altar.
an asherah. A tree used for idolatry.
God. A judge (see below 4:4).
to stand before him. In order to honor him.
and that if they refrain from judging, the order will be spoiled. The order of law and justice will be harmed because cases will not be judged properly.
and they press him. They urge him.
and likewise the seventy elders, Moses our teacher ordained them and the Divine Presence rested upon them. See Numbers 11:16-17, 24-25.

up to the court of Joshua, up to the court of Moses our teacher. Only the ordained may ordain. Thus every ordination derives from Joshua son of Nun, who was ordained by Moses our teacher, or from Moses our teacher directly.

and whether one is ordained by the Nasi or by one of the ordained, etc.. There is no difference whether a person is ordained by the Nasi of the Sanhedrin or by another ordained person, even if the one who ordained him never actually sat in the Sanhedrin.
not that they lay their hands on the head of the elder. As Moses did to Joshua.
even cases of fines. Which can be judged only by experts (below 5:8).
by three, provided that one of them is ordained by others. At least three are needed to ordain the judge; only one of them must himself be ordained, and the two who join him may be unordained.
only a judge is called 'God', etc.. This is what the Torah calls judges (see for example Exodus 22:8 and Targum Onkelos there, and see Guide of the Perplexed 2:6).
and they established them as experts. They determined that they were experts.
to the house of Hillel the Elder. Who was Nasi of the Sanhedrin.

and that the Nasi should not ordain unless the Av Beit Din is with him, and the Av Beit Din should not, etc.. In order to honor the Av Beit Din as well (the second most important judge in the Great Sanhedrin, above 1:3), they enacted that the Nasi himself ordains only together with the Av Beit Din, and the Av Beit Din ordains only together with the Nasi.
elders. Sages.

and the whole Land of Israel that those who came up from Egypt took possession of is fit for ordination. The whole area conquered by those who came up from Egypt was sanctified with the sanctity of the Land of Israel. This sanctity lapsed with the exile, and only the smaller area held by those who returned from Babylon was sanctified for all time (see Hilchot Terumot 1:5), but for the purpose of ordaining judges the whole area held by those who came up from Egypt is considered the Land of Israel and is fit for ordination (see Radbaz; and see Hilchot Terumot there, halachah 7, which details the borders of the Land of those who came up from Egypt).
for particular matters. That he be ordained only for certain matters, as explained below.
provided that he is fit for all matters. That in terms of his Torah knowledge he can rule on the whole Torah.

and to give him authority to judge but not to rule on prohibition and permission, etc.. Ordination gives the ordained person authorization to deal with the area for which he was ordained. And although even a sage who has not received authorization may rule on some of the matters mentioned here (such as prohibition and permission), the ordained sage does not have to pay if he errs and causes damage by his ruling (Lechem Mishneh).

to permit firstborn animals because of their blemish. A firstborn of a pure animal is sanctified for the altar from birth, but if it has a blemish it is disqualified from the altar and permitted for eating (Hilchot Bechorot 1:3), and only an expert who has received authorization may determine that its blemish permits it for eating (ibid. 3:1).
to examine stains. To distinguish whether the color of the stain is that of impure niddah blood or a pure color (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 5:7-12).
to give authorization for a time. After this time his ordination lapses, and he will be forbidden to judge or rule.
an outstanding sage. In terms of his wisdom he is fit for ordination.
who was blind in one eye. Therefore he is disqualified from judging in the Sanhedrin, but he is fit to judge monetary cases (above 2:9).
they do not ordain him for monetary cases. Only if he was ordained before he became blind can he continue to judge monetary cases afterwards.
and afterwards he and the seventy will become the Great Court and ordain other courts. As above, 2:8.

it seems to me that if they agree, etc.. In the Commentary on the Mishnah (Sanhedrin 1:3) the Rambam bases his view on God's promise to restore the judges as at first. Since it is impossible to appoint judges who are not ordained, and no ordained person now remains, ordained from person to person back to Moses our teacher, we must say there is some way in which ordination can be renewed even not through an ordained person.

if so, why were the sages distressed about ordination, etc.. The sages of Israel made great efforts, at risk and with self-sacrifice, to prevent a situation in which no ordained judges would remain and cases of fines would lapse (see Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 14a).
because Israel is scattered, etc.. As a result it is impossible for all to agree, and it would be very difficult to renew ordination; but if ordained judges remained, they could easily ordain others.

and the matter requires a decision. There is doubt about the possibility of renewing ordination (Radbaz, Lechem Mishneh and others; and see Yad Peshutah, who explained that in order to renew ordination all the sages of Israel must agree to assemble to choose the ordained one, to stand as a quorum, and to decide by majority).
for the Sanhedrin is in force in the Land and outside the Land. Only ordination is limited to the Land of Israel, but the ordained judge outside the Land just as they judge in the Land.

the Exilarchs in Babylonia. The rule of the kings of the house of David continued also during the exile in Babylonia. The Exilarch was of royal descent (a descendant of the house of David), and received from the Persian and Babylonian authorities the leadership of the internal government of the Jews within the kingdom's territory.

they stand in place of a king and have the right to rule, etc.. Like a king they have the power to compel the people to whatever they wish and to judge them, and by this power they can authorize judges to judge even against the will of the litigants.
whether in the Land or outside the Land. The authority of the Exilarchs is not limited by place.
although he does not judge cases of fines. Since he was ordained by the Exilarch and not by ordained judges in the Land.

he may judge in all the Land of Israel and in the towns on the borders, etc.. These places are subject to the court of the Land of Israel, and the judges ordained by them judge in them by compulsion. But those outside the Land are not subject to the court of the Land of Israel, and they cannot be judged by compulsion by virtue of a court of the Land of Israel.
although he may judge cases of fines outside the Land. Since he was ordained by ordained judges in the Land of Israel.
who transgressed, and the Exilarch gave him authorization. He transgressed a negative commandment, as explained above 3:8.
the authorization is of no avail to him at all. He is not to be honored at all (ibid.), and his judgments are not judgments (below 6:4).

for one who consecrates a blemished animal for the altar, no sanctity takes effect on it. Just as a blemished animal cannot be consecrated (when one consecrates it, the sanctity of the body does not take effect but only the sanctity of its value, Hilchot Issurei Mizbe'ach 1:10), so an unfit person cannot be appointed judge.

a king is appointed only by a court of seventy-one. This refers to his initial appointment, and then a prophet is also needed. But a king who is the son of a king needs no appointment (see Hilchot Melachim 1:3 and the commentary there; and see Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 4:15, that the appointment of the High Priest is also done by seventy-one).

and they do not make a lesser Sanhedrin for each and every tribe. In addition to the commandment to appoint a Sanhedrin in each and every city (above 1:1), a Sanhedrin must be appointed in each tribe to judge its tribe (Sefer HaMitzvot, positive commandment 176, and see Hilchot Shegagot 13:1).
a tribe that was entirely led astray. To worship idols. Since they are many, they are judged by the Great Sanhedrin (see Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 16a).
a false prophet. He is liable to death and is judged by the Great Sanhedrin (see also Hilchot Avodah Zarah 5:9).
nor the High Priest in capital cases. See also Hilchot Kelei HaMikdash 5:8.

a rebellious elder. An ordained sage who reached the level of ruling and ruled and acted against the ruling of the Great Sanhedrin is liable to death; he is brought up from his city to the Great Sanhedrin in Jerusalem and executed there (see also Hilchot Mamrim 3:8).

they punish an apostate city. A city most of whose inhabitants were led astray and worshiped idols: the worshipers are killed by the sword, and they are judged by the Great Sanhedrin (see Hilchot Avodah Zarah 4:3, 4:6).
they give the sotah to drink. Hilchot Sotah 3:1.

they add to the city and to the courts. When they wish to enlarge the area of Jerusalem or of the Temple courts, a court of seventy-one must decide on it. The decision is made together with a king, a prophet, and the Urim and Tummim (Hilchot Beit HaBechirah 6:11).

they send out for a discretionary war. When the king wishes to wage a war to expand Israel's borders and enlarge the renown of the kingdom, he needs the agreement of the Great Sanhedrin (Hilchot Melachim 5:2, where it is explained that in an obligatory war no court permission is needed).

and for measuring the slain. When a person is found slain on the road and it is not known who killed him, judges are sent from the Great Sanhedrin to measure the distance to the surrounding cities and determine which city is nearest and must bring the broken-necked heifer. Although only five judges take part in the measuring (Hilchot Rotzeach 9:1 and below, halachah 5), their sending is done by authority of the whole Sanhedrin (Lechem Mishneh).

every great matter they shall bring to you. The judges appointed in the time of Moses our teacher were commanded to bring the cases concerning great matters to him, so all the great matters listed here must be brought to the Great Sanhedrin, which stands in the place of Moses our teacher and the seventy elders (above 1:3).
capital cases of a person. A person who committed a transgression and was sentenced to death.
an ox to be stoned. An ox that killed a person is liable to death by stoning (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 10:1).

an animal that was bred with or that bred with. When a man has relations with an animal or brings an animal upon himself, both the man and the animal are liable to death by stoning (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 1:16).

a lion, bear, leopard and panther that are domesticated and have owners. Predators that are accustomed and forewarned to do harm (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 1:6): when they are wild and ownerless they may be killed even without a court. But if they have owners who raised them at home, they are judged in court.
but a snake that killed someone, one kills it. So that it will not continue to do harm, it is killed without a court.

one who spreads an evil name. A husband claims that the girl he married committed adultery after her betrothal: if his words are found true she is stoned, and if he lied he is flogged and pays (Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 3:6).
they do not judge him first. When the husband comes to court to claim that his wife committed adultery (see also ibid., halachah 3).

the husband's words were not believed and the father came to sue him for the fine. His witnesses were disqualified, and it turns out he spread an evil name and must pay a fine to the girl's father, and there is no longer a capital case in this judgment.
although it is a matter of tradition, it says, etc.. Although the matter is learned from the tradition of the sages, it also has a hint in the verse.
and the congregation shall judge and the congregation shall save. The verses deal with the trial of one who killed unintentionally.
and a congregation is not fewer than ten. A congregation of men consists of at least ten people (as the Torah called the congregation of the spies, Mishnah Sanhedrin 1:6).

and they add three so that there will be, etc.. The decision to convict of a capital crime must be by a majority of at least two (below 8:1). So for the judging congregation to be able to convict, two more must be added against the saving congregation, and since the court must be able to weigh and decide by majority ('so that the court will be balanced' - see R. Yitzchak Shilat in Rambam Meduyak, and see further Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Sotah 9:1), the number of judges cannot be even, and one must be added to the twenty-two (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 1:6).
lashes by three. Cases of lashes, in which a transgressor is flogged.

even though he might die when they flog him. Although there is concern that the person might die from the lashes, this is not feared, since before the flogging they assess how many blows this person can receive without dying, and according to that they determine how many lashes he will receive (below 17:1).

the breaking of the heifer's neck by five. The measuring of the distance from the slain person to the surrounding cities, to determine the city that must bring the broken-necked heifer, is done by five judges (see above, halachah 1).

the intercalation of the month by three. Examining the witnesses who testify to seeing the moon, and sanctifying the month on their testimony, is done by three judges (see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 2:8).

the intercalation of the year by seven. Adding an extra month (Adar II) to the year so that Pesach will fall in the spring is done by seven judges (see Hilchot Kiddush HaChodesh 4:9-10, where it is explained that after the fact, if three intercalated it, the year is intercalated).
and all of these are ordained as we have explained. Above 4:1.
cases of fines. Fines are monetary obligations that do not coincide with the monetary loss caused to the claimant (see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 2:8).

such as robberies. For example, when a robber denies the accusation against him and swears to it, he must pay the principal plus a fifth (Hilchot Gezelah 7:1-2). That addition is a fine, but the principal is not a fine, and judges who are not experts also judge it (see below, halachah 13, and Mirkevet HaMishneh there).

and injuries. Payments for damage, pain and shame that one who injures his fellow must pay (see Hilchot Chovel 1:1). However, payment of 'loss of work' for idleness and payment of healing are not fines, and judges who are not experts also judge them (as below, halachah 10).
and the payments of double and of four and five times. Which the thief pays (Hilchot Genevah 1:4, 1:6).
and the rapist and the seducer. Who pay a fine for raping or seducing a girl (Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 1:1).
three experts, who are the ordained in the Land of Israel. Above 4:1.
admissions and loans. A case of a person who admitted that he owes his fellow money or borrowed money from him.
and even a single expert judges them. For in monetary cases a court of three is not required, and an individual is permitted to judge (see above 2:10-11).
although the court outside the Land is not 'God'. For they are not ordained (above 4:4).

they act as agents of the court of the Land of Israel. The judges outside the Land serve as substitutes for the ordained judges of the Land of Israel (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Kamma 8:1).
and they involve a monetary loss. For the claim is for money that the claimant lost.
the fines that the sages fixed. Cases in which the sages set a fixed amount for the fine.
for one who strikes his fellow, or slaps his fellow, and the like. See Hilchot Chovel 3:9.
one who pays half damages. For example, a tam ox that did damage by goring, where this payment is a fine.

except for half damages of pebbles. When an animal in walking kicks up clods of earth and the like with its feet and does damage, the owners pay half the damage. Although payment for damage by pebbles is half damage, it is not in the category of a fine (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 2:7).

everything is assessed as a slave. The payment for 'damage' that one who injures a person pays, which is determined by calculating how much this person would have sold for as a slave before the injury and how much he can be sold for now (Hilchot Chovel 1:2). This payment is defined as a fine and is not judged by judges who are not experts (see Mirkevet HaMishneh below, halachah 14).

a person who injured his fellow, etc.. The injurer must pay the injured five things: damage, pain, shame, loss of work and healing. Payments of damage, pain and shame are considered fines and are not collected by judges who are not experts. But payments of healing and loss of work (compensation for idleness during the illness) are money and not a fine, and are collected even by judges outside the Land (see Hilchot Chovel 5:7).
an animal that did damage with tooth and foot. It ate for its own enjoyment or did damage in the course of walking.

since it is forewarned for them from the start. Every animal is accustomed to do damage in this way ('forewarned'), and so the owner pays full damages already the first time it did damage (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 1:2).

if it was a tam and became forewarned and did damage, etc.. When it did damage in a way that is not its usual way, it is defined as a tam and the owner pays half damages, and this damage is not collected outside the Land since it is a fine (above, halachah 9). If it became accustomed to doing so many times, it became forewarned for this damage and the owner pays full damages (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 1:4). But outside the Land an animal cannot be made forewarned (for the reason explained in the next halachah), so there is no way to judge payment for its damages. And even if a forewarned ox that was made forewarned in a court of the Land of Israel is brought, its damages are not judged outside the Land, since this is not a common case.
such as if it bit or gored, etc.. These five things ('damages of the horn') are the cases in which the animal is a tam from the start (ibid. 1:5).
pushed. Pushed with its body intentionally.
because one must testify about it before a court. See also Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 6:2.
if the court was outside the Land. Having been ordained in the Land and gone out of the Land.
just as they judge cases of fines outside the Land. Above 4:12.

so they warn the animal before them outside the Land. And although the animal becomes forewarned, judges outside the Land who are not ordained cannot judge its damages, since this case is not common (Radbaz, Kesef Mishneh).
the principal. The amount that he stole or robbed.
the addition. The payments of double and four and five times that the thief is liable for, and the fifth added by one who denied a robbery he committed and swore falsely (Mirkevet HaMishneh).

and not everyone who pays on his own admission is collected from by the judges outside the Land. Only a monetary obligation is collected on the debtor's admission, but one who admits to a fine is exempt from payment (Hilchot Genevah 1:5). However, there are things for which one who admits is liable and yet they are not collected outside the Land.
the indignity and the shame. Paid by one who raped or seduced a virgin girl, and one who admits to seducing a virgin girl pays them on his own admission (Hilchot Na'arah Betulah 2:12).
and the ransom. Paid by the owner of a forewarned ox that killed a person (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 10:4).
the judges outside the Land do not collect it. Because they are not common or there is no monetary loss in them (Radbaz).
cases of indirect causation. The liability of one who causes his fellow a monetary loss to pay (Hilchot Chovel UMazik 7:7).

one who hands over his fellow's property. One who hands his fellow's property over to a violent person who robs the property must pay his fellow, even if he did not hand over the property to the violent person with his own hands but showed him where the property was (Hilchot Chovel UMazik 8:1).

they excommunicate him until he appeases his opponent. They instituted this so that a sinner should not profit and to prevent people from harming one another (Teshuvot HaGeonim, Sha'arei Tzedek 4, gate 1, sec. 2 and sec. 14).
he goes up with him to judgment in the Land of Israel. And there they will judge the fine he must pay in a court of ordained judges.

and once he gives him the amount fitting for him, they lift his excommunication, etc.. If the litigant is not willing to be appeased with the money the court assesses he should receive but demands more, they lift the excommunication in any case.
the injured party seized. Took it himself, not through a court.
an individual who is an expert recognized by the public, although he judges monetary cases alone. Above 2:11.

an admission before him is not an admission in court. An admission before a single expert does not have the standing of an admission before a court. For example, regarding writing a document on the basis of the admission: if he admitted before a court of three they can write a promissory note on it, but if he did not admit before three they do not write a document (see Hilchot Toen VeNitan 7:3-4).

and likewise one who denies before them and afterwards witnesses came is established as a denier. After it becomes clear through witnesses that the claim he first made before three was false, he must pay and his other claims are not believed (see Hilchot Toen VeNitan 6:1). But when he denied before a single judge he is not established as a denier and is believed on other claims.

and he cannot go back and claim, as we have explained. When he made a claim in court and left, he cannot return and make a different claim (ibid. 7:8). But if he claimed before a single judge, he can return and claim even after leaving his presence.
the judgment is reversed. The judgment is annulled.
a strongman. A violent man, from whom what was paid to him cannot be recovered.
and fed it to the dogs. Because of the judge's ruling forbidding the meat, the litigant gave the meat to the dogs and suffered a loss.
although he caused damage, he did not intend to damage. Although generally one who causes damage must pay (Hilchot Chovel UMazik 7:7), here since the judge did not intend to damage, he is exempt.

an expert. One versed in the laws, whether he is an expert recognized by the public (whose greatness in Torah is well known to the public) even though not ordained, or an expert to the court that ordained him (see Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Bechorot 4:3).
and takes authorization from the Exilarch. For it is within the Exilarch's authority to appoint a judge who will judge the litigants against their will (above 4:14).

but the litigants accepted him upon themselves, since he is an expert, etc.. When the litigants accepted him upon themselves and in addition he is an expert, the judgment is reversed, and if it cannot be reversed he is exempt from paying. But if one of these conditions is lacking, the law is different, as below, halachah 3.

whether one who takes authorization from the Exilarch, etc.. The law of one who takes authorization from the Exilarch is the same as that of one who takes authorization from a court in the Land of Israel, except that one who takes authorization from the Exilarch may judge against the will of the litigants anywhere in the world, whereas one who takes authorization from a court in the Land of Israel may judge only in the Land of Israel and not outside it.
as we have explained. Above 4:14.

an expert of the court who did not take authorization. Who was ordained by a court but did not receive authorization from them to judge (see above 4:8). Although he was ordained, since he did not receive authorization to judge he must pay from his own house (and all the more so an expert recognized by the public who was not ordained pays from his own house - see Yad Peshutah and the note of R. Yitzchak Shilat in Rambam Meduyak).

if he carried out the transaction by hand, what he did is done, and he pays from his own house. When he himself carried out the judgment and took money from the defendant and gave it to the plaintiff, since the error is not absolute the judgment is not annulled, and the litigant who won through the error need not return. And since the judge had not received authorization to judge this case, he must pay the litigant who lost. (But when he has authorization to judge, he has authorization to reverse the judgment even after carrying out the transaction by hand.)

and if he did not carry out the transaction by hand, the judgment is reversed. When he did not carry out the judgment with his own hands, he can reverse the judgment even in a case of error in judgment.
even though he took authorization. The authorization to judge given by the Exilarch or by a court of the Land of Israel is of no avail to one not fit to judge (above 4:15).
among the powerful men. Who take money by force.

he must pay from his own house and then take back from this litigant to whom he gave improperly. Since he is not considered a judge at all and his judgment is not a judgment, he must return what he took improperly from the litigant. He may, however, sue the other litigant (who received money improperly) to return to him what was given to him.
and if he has nothing to return, etc.. Even when the litigant has nothing with which to repay the judge what was improperly given, the judge pays.
who declared impure. Pure foods on the basis of the ruling of a non-expert judge who ruled that they are impure.

he pays, as does anyone who causes damage, since he intends to do damage. Since he is not a judge and has no authorization at all to judge this case, we regard his acts as done with deliberate intent to damage, and he pays even though he did not damage directly but only caused a loss by his ruling (see Hilchot Chovel UMazik 7:7).
and afterwards he learned that he was not subject to an oath. It became known that the judge erred and he should not have had to swear.
that they acquired from him for the compromise. They gave binding force to the compromise by a kinyan sudar (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5 and the commentary there).
and any acquisition in error is reversible. See Hilchot Mechirah 15:1-3.
who grew stubborn in the judgment. Who argued and quarreled in the case.
to the Great Court. In Jerusalem.
write and give me for what reason you judged me. He wants to go with the writing to the Great Court and see whether they agree.

they write and give it to him and afterwards take from him. Although he wants to go with the writing to the Great Court, they do not wait to see whether they will reverse the judgment, but immediately take from him the money he must pay (Hagahot Maimoniyot).

and if a matter needs to be asked of the Great Court in Jerusalem, they write, etc.. The judges submit their doubts in writing to the Great Court and judge according to its reply, and do not send the litigants to litigate there.

in other cases where this one claims and that one claims. When both parties sue each other in court, for example a case between partners, or when two dispute to whom a certain item belongs and neither is more in possession than the other (see Taz, Choshen Mishpat 14:1).
proof. For example, a promissory note.
an empty claim. Without support.
he swears in his place and is released. Like a defendant who denies the entire claim, who must take the oath of heset and be released by it (Hilchot Toen VeNitan 1:3).

for through this the judgment will come out true. For each judge will argue in favor of the litigant who chose him, and through this all sides of the merit of both litigants will become clear (see Kesef Mishneh).

a relative or disqualified person. A relative who is disqualified from testifying (Hilchot Edut 13:1), or one of the other people disqualified from testifying (see ibid. 9:1). All of these are also disqualified from judging (ibid. 16:4).

whether to be a judge or to be a witness against him. That he accepted upon himself to follow the ruling this judge will give as if he were a qualified judge, or to accept the testimony of this witness as if he were a qualified witness.

even if he accepted one of those disqualified for a transgression as two witnesses, etc.. Even if that person was disqualified because he committed a transgression (see ibid. 10:1-2), and he accepted his testimony as the testimony of two witnesses, or accepted that he would judge alone and his judgment would be considered the judgment of three qualified judges.
if they acquired from him on this. He strengthened his acceptance of the disqualified person by a kinyan sudar (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5 and the commentary there).
he may retract. He can retract.
and said to him, swear to me by your life. Instead of taking a severe oath in the name of God as required in an oath in court (see Hilchot Shevuot 11:8).
the judgment was concluded and he swore. He swore by his life as his opponent agreed.

and the same law applies to one who was obligated to take the oath of heset and reversed it. The Talmudic sages instituted that one who denies the entire claim against him and is exempt from an oath by Torah law swears a light oath called the oath of heset (Hilchot Toen VeNitan 1:3). This oath can be reversed onto the plaintiff, so that instead of the defendant swearing and being released, he can demand that the plaintiff swear on his claim and take what he claims (ibid., halachah 6).
he may retract until the judgment is concluded and he swears. And once he swore as agreed, his opponent cannot retract.
proof. For example, a document.
he closed his claims. He closed the possibility of making a new claim.
his apundah. A garment worn next to the flesh that absorbs sweat (Rambam's Commentary on the Mishnah, Sanhedrin 3:8).
and they pay no attention to his witnesses or his proof. For we suspect there is fraud in these witnesses or proofs, since he already said he has no witnesses or proofs (ibid.).
the skin bag. A leather container.
and claims came against him because of his predecessor. For example, they claimed from him a debt that the one he inherited from owed.

one from whom they acquired, etc.. A person who was obligated to take an oath in court, and they agreed with him by kinyan that he would swear by a certain date and that if he did not swear he would lose his right (to claim that he is not liable or that his fellow owes him).
and he swears when his fellow sues him as it was before. As the law was before they made the kinyan.

and in other cases of prohibition and permission, impure and pure, and the like. In these too the Sanhedrin decides by majority, and its decision binds even those who dissent (see Hilchot Mamrim chapter 1).
and if the majority convict, he is not executed unless those who convict outnumber those who acquit by two. And see below 9:2 for how the case is decided when there is a majority of one to convict.
from hearsay. The tradition of the sages in the expositions of the verses.

for the Torah warned about this and said, Do not follow the majority to do evil, etc.. In this way the commandment to follow the majority is reconciled with the warning not to follow the many to do evil: to convict one does not follow a small majority but a majority of at least two.
that they incline greatly and those who convict are two. More than those who acquit.
a court of three. Who do not judge capital cases.
